sentences.text: Most Orodus species are known primarily from their rounded, ridge-covered teeth, which were adapted for crushing prey. Fossil evidence shows that these animals lacked dorsal fin spines, possessed small pectoral fins, and had teeth that varied in shape based on their position in the mouth.
The largest species, O. ramosus, had teeth about 11 cm wide, leading to size estimates of 12 to 15 meters, though these figures are considered unreasonable by researchers.
The genus Orodus was originally described by Agassiz in 1838, with De Koninck cited as the parent authority for the genus in 1878.
The species O. greggi grew to approximately 2 to 4 meters in length, while O. micropterygius reached about 1 meter.
Orodus is classified within the class Chondrichthyes and is thought to be most closely related to living chimaeras among orodontiforms.

Orodus fossils have been found in Europe, Asia, and North America dating from the late Devonian to the Late Carboniferous periods. The time range for Orodus spans from the Frasnian to the Wordian, between 382.31 and 264.9 million years ago.
